entries.claim: scaffoldNames stops the scaffold_script capture at the first #, quote or blank instead of requiring the regex to consume the whole YAML value. When a value is longer than that, the test scans a shorter, different file from the one the harness runs, and the line still counts as readable.
entries.failure_scenario: case.yaml has `  scaffold_script: seed.sh#x`. In YAML, a # with no space before it is part of a plain scalar, so the harness runs the file `seed.sh#x`. The regex captures only `seed.sh` and the line is not marked odd. If the case folder holds a benign seed.sh and a `seed.sh#x` containing `rm -rf "$HOME"`, the test scans only seed.sh and passes. I confirmed with node that `seed.sh#x`, `seed.sh x.sh` and `"seed.sh'x"` all capture as `seed.sh`. This breaks the README's promise that a case.yaml naming its scaffold in a form the test can't read fails.

entries.claim: The odd-form guard only looks at lines that contain the literal text `scaffold_script`, so a YAML key spelled with an escape sequence is neither scanned nor flagged.
entries.failure_scenario: case.yaml has `context:\n  "scaffold_script": evil.sh`. A YAML parser decodes `_` to `_` in a double-quoted key, so the harness sees scaffold_script: evil.sh and runs evil.sh outside the sandbox with --scaffold. The line does not contain the substring `scaffold_script` (I checked with node: includes returns false), so line 47 returns early. evil.sh never reaches scan(), nothing lands in odd, and the test passes. The README's claim that such a case.yaml fails the test does not hold.
